 I. Topic Background 
 Literacy education is an exponentially important part of a child's development and 
 dictates everything from a child's mental health to schooling and job opportunities, and although 
 Latvia does not have issues with this (Latvia's literacy rate is 99.89%  1  ), surrounding countries do. 
 Countries that struggle with lower literacy rates and levels of literacy are likely to deal with 
 higher crime rates, lowered workforce productivity leading to a massive loss in tax revenue, and 
 a higher risk of mental health issues which end up costing trillions of dollars globally.  2  Parents 
 with below-average literacy levels have 72% of children with literacy issues.  3  In addition, 
 children and parents who have low literacy levels have higher hospitalization rates due to the 
 lack of engagement and adherence to health services and medical advice such as cancer and 
 other disease screening.  4  Multiple studies have consistently revealed links between literacy and 
 infant mortality rates because of malnutrition and lack of proper vaccination.  5  In 1999, studies

 throughout rural and Urban areas of Latvia, 79% of Latvians have a below-average health

 increased likelihood of disease development that causes higher mortality rates. This low health

 regular users of drugs such as opioids and amphetamines.  12  In 2012 there were 170 known 
 drug-induced deaths in Estonian which is up from 101 from two years earlier.  13  Children living

 under.  15  With such a large number of children living in poverty, receiving a quality education is 
 of the utmost importance. Latvia has already seen a decrease in poverty from 2008 to 2012 as the 
 poverty rate dropped from 26.3% which seems to be due mostly to the fact that primary as well 
 as secondary education became free and obligatory.  16  The main reason that the poverty rates still 
 continue to lie at such a high rate is mainly due to discrimination in the Latvian education 
 system.  17  Romani and Russian speakers are victims of major language barriers since most 
 Latvian schools do not offer to teach in these languages. Additionally, there is sort of a “separate 
 but equal society” where Romani and some Russian children are forced to attend different 
 classes than their fellow students which reinforces the belief that they are not capable of 
 sharing education with their Latvian peers. The European Commission Against Racism and 
 Intolerance (ICRI) has decided to work on the issues and has promised that the Latvian 
 The education system will change its curriculum to include instruction in minority languages as 
 well as fight to end the separation of ethnicities in classes.

 Cultural Organization (UNESCO) considers a “high literacy rate”.  Latvia values literacy and 
 education as essential tools for daily life, 90% of Latvian adults have completed a secondary 
 education which is much higher than the average European country. For reference,  The 
 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) average is 75% and the 
 Group of Twenty (G20) average is 60%.  18  Latvia’s main  way of testing for literacy is the OECD 
 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), anything around the OECD average 
 score of 487 is considered an adequate literacy level, and anything above that is considered 
 exceptional. Latvia in addition to other Baltic states does have struggles with discrimination in 
 the education system against minority ethnicities such as Russians, Belarussians, Polish, and 
 Ukrainians.  19  Only 40 percent of Latvian primary schools  offer to teach Russian which does not 
 line up since 24% of the Latvian population speak Russian.  20  The Latvian government is working 
 to vote through legislation to raise this number in the coming years which the government thinks 
 will help improve end-of-high-school exam results that are only given in Latvian, a language that 
 shares very little with Russian.  21  Latvia has decided  to set aside 3.3 million pounds (3.82 million 
 U.S. dollars) from European Union (EU) structural funds to help at least 2,700 teachers improve

 make the money inadequate. Additionally, Both Lithuania and Latvia hope to increase their 
 media literacy level by adding explicit mentions of media and information literacy into their 
 general School curriculum. This addition of curriculum regarding critical analysis of media 
 content is expected to “reduce one-direction influence of mass media communication allowing to 
 identify and prevent the distribution of biased information”.  22  Lithuania whose media literacy 
 level was tested for the first time in 2017 and had a level of 37.8 percent and hoped to raise that 
 to 41.3 percent by the year 2023.  23  With the Baltic region having some of the best literacy rates 
 worldwide, it is easy to see how much value they find in literacy education, Latvia, although 
 having an outstanding literacy rate still has issues in its education system that they hope to end in 
 the coming years.

 everyone has the right to education. Latvia ensures that every child may acquire integrated 
 primary education and lower secondary education free of charge. The main aim of the education 
 policy in Latvia is “to provide quality educational opportunities for all residents of Latvia to

 Latvia provides a legal entitlement to early childhood education and care (ECEC) for all children 
 past the age of 18 months. Municipalities are obligated to ensure that any Latvian citizen has 
 access to an ECEC station close to their home. As stated previously, Latvia has issues with 
 discrimination of minorities in the educational system and scores below the OECD average in 
 reading. In recent years Latvia has increased its total general government expenditure on 
 education (% of GDP) from 4.2% in 2018 to 6% as of 2020.  25  The Latvian teacher salaries have 
 had massive increases in recent years because of this increase in expenditure, from 2015 to 2021 
 Latvia increased its teacher salaries by an exponential 59%.  26  Still, Latvia's teacher salaries are 
 still relatively low at an average of 29,169 USD compared to the 50,026 of the OECD countries. 
 27  Although this jump in salaries might seem minuscule, it is still a leap towards helping better 
 minor education issues that Latvia is facing. In 2018, the Latvian Parliament approved 
 amendments to the Education Law and the Law on General Education that

 works towards a gradual transition to a mostly Latvian secondary education. Starting in the 
 2022-2023 school year, all general education subjects in upper-secondary programs will be 
 taught only in the Latvian language excluding foreign language classes. 
 The Delegation of Latvia believes that bilingual teachers or teachers with knowledge of a 
 second language should be hired, as of 2018 only 60 percent of schools in Latvia were taught in 
 the Latvian language leaving 40 percent of schools being taught in minority languages like 
 Russian.  28  This becomes a major issue with end-of-high  school exams because they are only 
 given in Latvian which causes half of Latvia's students to struggle with the exams. By hiring 
 bilingual teachers and putting money into training to speak across different languages, Latvia can 
 help transition the many minority language schools to having more of their general education 
 material in Latvian to help break the language barrier that is causing discrimination in the 
 education system. The Latvian school districts can do this by offering benefits for teachers who 
 have taken their own time to learn and educate themselves on a second language. Greater health 
 benefits that cover a wider range of issues are big motivational factors for almost any type of job. 
 In a study done by Fractl in 2016, over 90% of employees would rather take a low-paying job 
 with higher-quality health benefits than a higher-paying job with a lack of health benefits.  29

 Bilingualism is additionally linked with many positive effects such as having better creativity 
 and flexibility as well as being more open-minded to ideas which are essential traits for any 
 teacher. 
 Latvia can also raise awareness of Latvian citizens’ legal entitlement to ECEC for any 
 children past the age of 18 months. The delegation of Latvia believes that raising awareness of 
 their ECEC programs will help improve children's Latvian literacy levels in future years. If 
 children start to begin to learn and be introduced to the Latvian language at a young age, they 
 will need less exposure to it in primary and secondary education which helps prevent the 
 problem of language barrier discrimination before it even has time to start. Learning a language 
 at a young age is proven to have many benefits such as greater confidence, higher and more 
 advanced reading skills in primary and secondary education, and higher test and exam results.  30 
 This will help improve the Latvian reading test levels where they score below the OECD average 
 on. Learning a language at an earlier age also allows more future job opportunities which allows 
 for a stronger economy and more money to be put towards helping better the Latavin education 
 system. We believe if these strategies are implemented in the Latvian community, there will be 
 advances in the fight against discrimination and language issues in the Latvian education system.

 Latvia can also raise awareness of Latvian citizens’ legal entitlement to ECEC for any 
 children past the age of 18 months. The delegation of Latvia believes that raising awareness of 
 their ECEC programs will help improve children's Latvian literacy levels in future years. If 
 children start to begin to learn and be introduced to the Latvian language at a young age, they 
 will need less exposure to it in primary and secondary education which helps prevent the 
 problem of language barrier discrimination before it even has time to start. Learning a language 
 at a young age is proven to have many benefits such as greater confidence, higher and more 
 advanced reading skills in primary and secondary education, and higher test and exam results.  30

 on. Learning a language at an earlier age also allows more future job opportunities which allows 
 for a stronger economy and more money to be put towards helping better the Latavin education 
 system. We believe if these strategies are implemented in the Latvian community, there will be 
 advances in the fight against discrimination and language issues in the Latvian education system.
